intro: Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen constraints, and the game has to honour all of them. Tonight's roll was seed 4255480681: a loudspeaker in a tiny hat, distilling eggs, for comfort. Here is how that became a village cricket ground, a hen run and a mortar.

rolls.value: a loudspeaker in a tiny hat
rolls.became: Reg, the loudspeaker on the pavilion roof, who has called forty seasons of village cricket and commentates everything, including itself. The tiny knitted hat has been on its horn for years. Nobody remembers who knitted it.

Egg oil, oleum ovorum, is a real old apothecary remedy: hard-boiled yolks, worked until the oil sweats out. The pavilion's almanac (1703) prescribes it for a raw throat. The copper still does the slow version; the mortar does the quick one.
Every cricket ground has a tea, and every cricket tea has egg sandwiches, so there are hens behind the pavilion. Reg's medicine has been in the coop the whole time.
The yolks have to be rubbed round a mortar, so you rub. Once the season opens you also rub the cricket ball shiny on the bowler's trousers, which is what bowlers actually do.
Drops of egg oil: one a rub at first, millions by the last dose. The coop's hens get into the thousands, which the egg-and-cress sandwiches can confirm.
Reg's throat is raw. Ten doses of egg oil fill its Comfort, and each one leaves its voice a little smoother and a little softer (listen to the calls).
Maud Pettigrew of the Gazette, who reviews Reg every match and has never given more than one star. Her complaint is always the same, if you read it closely: too loud.
Maud. The whole game is drawn in her reporter's notebook, in ballpoint, because she's at every match and she doodles.

rolls.value: it gets undone, and that's fine
rolls.became: The Final can be rained off. If it is, nobody wins the cup, the ink in Maud's notebook runs down the page, and nobody minds: it was only a drawing, and Reg finally has nothing to say.
About an hour and a half, over a sitting or two. While you're away the coop keeps laying and the twelfth man keeps bowling, gently. Nothing hatches without someone watching.

rolls.value: producers that make producers (tier 2 makes tier 1)
rolls.became: Hens lay eggs into the still. Broody hens hatch hens. Roosters keep the eggs fertile and set more hens broody (and crow over Reg's commentary, which Reg considers a rival broadcast).

rolls.value: a second, parallel game that opens midway
rolls.became: At Comfort 4 Reg is fit to call again and the cricket season opens beside the hen run: rub the ball, the bowler bowls, Reg calls it, the crowd cheers. Cheers have their own shop and their own fixture list, and both halves lead to the Final.
Sun, then rain, every couple of minutes. Rain stops play, but it keeps everyone in the coop, so hatching doubles. The best time to rub the mortar is when the covers are on.

rolls.value: a secret ending behind the obvious one
rolls.became: The obvious ending: call the winning runs of the Final, and Maud gives four stars ('much too loud'). The secret one: when the cloud comes over, pour Maud's tea instead. Reg stops talking, rain stops play, and Maud gives her first five-star review, to silence.

Every line wobbles and re-draws itself a few times a second, like a flip-book, on ruled paper with a red margin and the holes punched down the side. A few props are line icons redrawn with Rough.js so they look like the same pen.
Old paper and a teal ballpoint, with Maud's red pen for reviews, copper for the still and a dab of olive highlighter where something matters.

A harpsichord minuet in F lydian (the B natural is the lift). Alone in the hen yard, joined by continuo and a recorder for the season, and thinned back to the harpsichord when it rains. Every rub, drop and cheer is on the same scale.
Reg commentates everything: the pestle ('A LOVELY TURN!'), the hens ('a big unit'), the rain, and itself. Maud answers in red pen.
No calendar nod today: just cricket, which is timeless by design (some matches last five days).

outro: Forty seasons, one almanac, a lot of hens. Comfort was a long time coming, and it was quieter than Reg expected.
